“On that night the angels and the Spirit descend, by permission of their Lord, to carry out every command. And peace reigns until the breaking of dawn” (Quran 97:4–5).

“God showed me all the angels, each of them appearing in human form, smiling messengers of glad tidings. Among them was Gabriel, the most beautiful of the angels. Their braided hair was like that of women. Their faces were like the red rose. Some wore veils of light upon their heads; others wore crowns set with precious stones; still others were clothed in mantles of pearls. I saw them on several occasions, when they also had the appearance of beautiful youths.

“I saw the angel Rezwân (Ridwân) and Paradise, and I entered it. I saw the houris and the young attendants, whose appearance was as God describes it (see Quran 37:47; 56:17–22, etc.). I entered the heavenly palaces. I drank from the flowing waters and ate the fruits of the Garden. Many times I also saw the Throne (‘arsh) and the Korsî. And I saw God clothed in a form that gave him the appearance of a shaykh. He wore a Persian mantle. Then I felt myself melting away before his majesty and his bearing (§ 24).”
On another night, Ruzbihan contemplates God:

“Above the Throne, in the bridal chambers of intimacy, revealing Himself with the attributes of Beauty and Majesty. No one stood before Him except Gabriel, who was weeping and suddenly tore his garments in the violence of his frenzy of love before the divine Beauty. Some time passed… I saw rocks over which flowed a great river, like a river of pearls. I saw Khidr and Elijah, together with all the Abdâl, washing their clothes in the river. Never had I seen a sight more enchanting than the vision of them at that moment (L. 157b).”

Ruzbihan repeatedly confides to us his visionary journeys into Paradise. After the great vision in which he had been joined by the three archangels and the Prophet around the Kaaba, he passes through a long period of relaxation until morning approaches. Then ecstasy seizes him once more:

“I was shown a man in the middle of the sanctuary. He seemed to be carrying sand from that place to somewhere else, until a door appeared beneath the sand. That door was opened for me. I passed through it and entered beyond. I saw another man standing beneath the doorway. The first was Ishmael; the second was Rezwân.

“Then, having crossed the threshold, I saw Paradise, with its trees, its flowers, and its countless lights. I saw Muhammad and all the prophets, the Friends of God (Awliyâ’), the martyrs, and the angels. I saw a multitude of believers there. I saw nothing that resembled this world. There was only light upon light, radiance upon radiance, beauty upon beauty (§ 53).”

“Never have I seen anything more beautiful. There I saw the angels, the prophets, the houris, and the heavenly palaces. All were filled with divine Lights. Among the trees of Paradise I saw a tree of turquoise, resembling a palm tree. If that tree, in all its grace and beauty, were shown to the people of this world (ahl al-donyâ), they would all die of longing for it (§ 81).”
The visionary also contemplates his own family there:

“I saw my family in one of the paradises, before God, appearing as beautiful young people, for I saw everyone who kept company around God in the form of youthful beauty. Then I saw my family in one of the upper chambers of Paradise, before God. This upper chamber was made of red hyacinth. My family were seated near God, along a row of cushions. They seemed to be waiting for me. Then I heard His word resounding from the world of Mystery: ‘…those of their fathers and their spouses who have been righteous.’

“I reflected upon these words addressed to me inwardly, and returned to the beginning of the Quranic verse: ‘The gardens of Eden: they shall enter them, together with those of their fathers, their spouses, and their children who have been righteous; and the angels shall come to visit them, entering through every gate’ (13:23). I understood that this was good news for me. At dawn I sat watching for the rising of the eternal morning (§ 82).”

It is a commonplace of a certain kind of Christian argument against Islam to disparage the joys of the Quranic Paradise on the grounds that they appeal to the senses. It is therefore important to see how those joys are anticipated and inwardly experienced by spiritual seekers within Islam itself. Among them, the dilemma that torments the Christian ascetic’s conscience has never been felt in any comparable way.

The description of the joys of Paradise belongs to the wider problem of tanzîh and tashbîh: on the one hand, declaring God utterly beyond every attribute (tanzîh); on the other, affirming the correspondences that link the invisible and visible worlds (tashbîh). The point is neither to sacrifice one to the other nor to surrender to either.

The mystical soul finds peace by passing between them, remaining equally distant from—and equally close to—both. Such a reconciliation is probably possible only because Sufism is animated by a sense of theophany: the experience of the divine making itself present and perceptible. The problem lies at the very heart of Ruzbihan’s teaching about divine manifestations, just as it does in the thought of Ibn Arabi. On its resolution depends the possibility of tasting the sweetness and peace of divine love within human love.

But here we have more than a theoretical explanation. We have the experience itself, lived in a visionary state. In any case, these are not perceptions made through the physical senses in the ordinary world. They are perceptions of the imagination in the intermediate, imaginal world—the mundus imaginalis, a world of forms experienced inwardly as real, rather than merely imagined.

“I saw the Divine Presence (Hazrat) filled with angels of the highest rank, seated beneath the pavilions of Glory. I saw God. All the prophets and all the Messengers were seated, waiting beside the pulpit (minbar). When I had taken my seat at the pulpit and had spoken the words concerning the mutual recognition of spirits, the angels wept, and so did the prophets. And God was listening. A Light shone through His person, as though showing that He was in agreement with them. Then He said: ‘So it shall be on the Day of Resurrection.’

“Ah, shame upon anyone who thinks these revelations are mere fantasies to be suspected of tashbîh—of making God too human! Such a person is only a beginner. He has experienced nothing. He has never breathed the fragrance of the flowers of Paradise. These are experiences of the holy world, spiritual stations attained by those whose insight is deepest even as they remain most discerning. Such people know very well that these are forms in which divine Lordship (robobîya) appears: manifestations of the eternal Lights, forms taken by the divine Attributes through theophanies (§ 84).”
We know that Ruzbihan served for many years as a preacher in Shiraz. The passage just quoted shows him fulfilling the same role “in Heaven.”

Yet the subject of his preaching remains unchanged. We may recall the anecdote already mentioned at the end of Chapter II: when he first made his way through the ranks of his listeners to mount the pulpit in Shiraz, he stopped to admonish a mother whom he had just heard instructing her daughter to conceal her beauty beneath a veil. His preaching cannot help returning, on every occasion, to the mystery of the divine appearing through beauty.

The reverence and ethical demands that arise from this “manifestation of the divine” must never lose sight of what Ruzbihan calls iltibâs: the double meaning of the human Image, which at once is and is not what it appears to be. Everything accessible to the senses—everything visible or audible—has this double meaning.

What we can see reveals what cannot be seen; what we can hear reveals what cannot be heard. This is precisely the function of created beauty as a manifestation of the divine. Naturally, preaching such a doctrine may scandalize the devout defenders of orthodoxy: people who can sense no second meaning in the text of beauty, any more than in the revealed scripture. Ruzbihan himself can sometimes begin to doubt what he preaches.

But his visions restore his certainty. On the very night when he has contemplated the treasures of Paradise, he begins to meditate upon the immediate, direct vision permitted by the spiritual station of iltibâs, the twofold appearance of the divine. He is troubled by scruples. It is as though the demands of collective orthodoxy—the religion of legal rules and social conformity, which would impose a socially determined form upon faith—have risen again in his consciousness against his personal faith.

“I was troubling myself about what is eternal, trying to turn away from everything created. Then God appeared to me in the Holy Assembly (Majlis al-Qods), in a form so beautiful that every lover was captivated by it. He approached me and said: ‘Come now! There is no reason for you to distress yourself over this.’ I had the impression that He disliked my anxious effort to keep His transcendence apart from the forms perceived by the imagination.

“My heart was enchanted by this divine manifestation in a form suited to the secret of my love. And so I remained in ecstasy, sighing and weeping, until morning. Then, hour after hour, He revealed Himself to me under a new attribute, drawn from the hosts of pre-eternal Lights. When He had once more become invisible, I remembered what I had preached from the pulpit.
“But He said to me: ‘What you preached was indeed worthy of my secret. You preached it to guide created beings and to make known to them the beauty of the divine favours prepared for them’ (§ 83).”

When Ruzbihan speaks of God appearing “in a form suited to the secret of my love,” he gives us the secret of theophanies themselves. Each divine manifestation corresponds to the spiritual capacity of the person who receives it.

Yet precisely here the conflict reappears. These manifestations must necessarily be many and varied; each is like a distinct appearance of the divine. What becomes of this multiplicity when confronted with the absolute demand of tawhîd, the oneness of God? The conflict is indeed insoluble so long as we remain within an outward, literal understanding of monotheism, which places God before us as a transcendent object. The secret of esoteric tawhîd is that God is never an Object.

Rather, He is the active Subject of those acts through which created beings relate to Him. Such a truth can express itself only through paradox. These are the shath—the startling utterances of mystical ecstasy—from which Ruzbihan derives his title of shaykh shattâh, the master of ecstatic paradoxes.

The mystic himself becomes a paradox. It is not merely that he sometimes speaks in the first person, his human ego having withdrawn, and utters statements whose true subject can only be the Divine Being. His situation also compels him to challenge religion understood as a system of legal rules. He must accept, courageously and without concern for the judgment of others, that his wholly inward and personal religious life may appear outwardly impious or sacrilegious in the eyes of the Law and of organized religion. Such are the Sufis known as the Malâmatî, those willing to incur the blame of others.

The great mystical poet Hafez of Shiraz was one of them. As though to confirm the affinity that has already led us to see Ruzbihan as a precursor of Hafez, Ruzbihan tells us here that, in his youth, he had a Malâmatî shaykh. It is significant that this master should become the form of a divine manifestation in a vision that affirms the paradox of the many manifestations of the One and the identity of the Many.

“In my youth I had a shaykh. He was a master of great mystical knowledge, perpetually in a state of spiritual intoxication. He was a Malâmatî shaykh, whose true nature was unknown to ordinary people. One night I was contemplating a vast plain among the plains of Mystery. And behold, I saw God appearing in the likeness of this shaykh, at the entrance to the plain. I approached Him.

“Then He made a sign to me, pointing towards another plain. I went forward into that plain, and there again I saw a shaykh just like the first—and this shaykh was God. Once more He made a sign, pointing towards another plain. And so it continued until He had unveiled seventy thousand plains to me. Each time, at the entrance to each plain, I saw a figure resembling the one I had seen in the first.

“I said to myself: ‘And yet God Most High is unique, one, indivisible, beyond every number, great or small, beyond equals, opposites, and likenesses.’ Then it was said to me: ‘Such is the manifestation of the eternal Attributes, for they are without limit.’ At that moment I felt myself seized by the esoteric realities of tawhîd, rising from the sea of Magnificence (§ 34).”
Another account alludes to the same mystery:

“I saw a Light whiter than the brightness of pearls and snow… He revealed to me the beauties of the Attributes… No distance remained between Him and me. Then I saw in the divine Face such majesty and beauty that the inhabitants of Heaven and Earth might have died of delight. I saw that every region of Heaven and Earth was filled with them… He brought me into the station of the nearness of nearness. He showed me seventy thousand majesties, beauties, and perfections, and spoke words to me which, if the mountain of Qaf—the cosmic mountain—could hear them, would make it melt with pleasure…

“Then He seated me before Him and treated me with every kind of gracious attention. From His own hand He gave me a drink that I cannot describe. And I was allowed to hear things that I have no power to put into words (§ 47).”
The symbol of this drink returns in another vision, at the very moment when Ruzbihan, paradoxically, seems to wish to remind the Divine Being of His own transcendence.

“God lifted the veil from the angelic realm (malakût), assuming the form of Majesty and Beauty and revealing the whole series of Attributes corresponding to the human form. Then He showed me His Sublimity and Majesty in another spiritual station, and so it continued until I had contemplated Him in seventy stations, each time under an Attribute I had never seen before. Then He seated me at the Table of tender care, while I contemplated in Him colours of majesty that had never before entered my consciousness. He offered me food from that Table. I said: ‘My God!

“Yet surely You transcend the acts of eating and drinking! If the tears of repentance are the drink of angels, what, then, are the tears of longing and intimacy when one beholds You?’ Then He said to me: ‘That is my drink.’ Such is the tenderness with which He treats His prophets and His Friends, even while remaining transcendent above every attribute of created beings (L. 153b).”

The entire Diarium could be read as a series of variations on this theme of double meaning and direct vision: God clothes Himself in attributes corresponding to those of created beings (tashbîh), without contradicting the absolute transcendence of His pure Essence (tanzîh). For rational dialectic, there is no way out of this contradiction. Only pure love resolves it in actual experience. This is what Ruzbihan will learn through his visions and confirm through the experience of his life.

In the account in which he describes the veils of red roses and white roses beneath which he so often contemplated God, he admits that, had anyone been able to witness those intimate exchanges between himself and God, that witness would have recognized him as a zindîq—a heretic. This was a designation by which Islamic orthodoxy associated with the old Zoroastrian religion of Iran anything that seemed to violate the letter of the Law. How could the strict defender of orthodoxy understand that, beneath a divine form “suited to the secret of the mystic’s love,” the mystic perceives transcendent Majesty itself—precisely because that Majesty cannot in fact be perceived in any other way or anywhere else?

“What I describe, and what I allude to, are the embroideries woven by the symbols of the higher sciences of love. God reveals Himself within them under the attributes of Majesty and Beauty. He has invested them with this love and this mystical knowledge, because in the true Reality of tawhîd there is a sea of negation before which the prophets and the Messengers, the angels and the Friends of God, all flee. And in the mystical station of tawhîd burn the fires of Magnificence, which consume thought, understanding, and every form of perception (§ 39).”

Impenetrable is the mystery of the One who is utterly one. He can reveal Himself only by assuming a veil of clouds proportionate to the heart that receives Him, whether the heart of an angel or of a spiritual seeker. That veiling must at once be accepted and pierced.

“He appeared to me in the aspect of the Uncreated, from among the Orients of pre-eternity, and He said to me: ‘I have travelled towards you from the Mystery of Mysteries. Between you and me lies a distance of seven hundred thousand years…’ He treated me with tender consideration and said: ‘I have chosen you, in your time, for this rank above the worlds.’ He unveiled to me holy beauties and the particular qualities of the eternal Attributes. I contemplated a beauty within a majesty, and a majesty within a beauty, which I shall never be able to describe… In my youth I was accustomed to keeping vigil until deep into the night.

“Thus, one night, while I was praying, the Divine Being passed close to me, appearing in the most beautiful of forms. He smiled at me and threw little sachets of musk towards me. I said: ‘Give me a great many of them.’ He answered: ‘Each one is an angel, and you are an angel of Persia’ (§§ 21–22).”

Again and again, the mystic tries to force his way beyond this double meaning of appearances, to overcome it and attain absolute knowledge. Only later will he learn that it can be transcended only by being transfigured. Otherwise, he exposes himself to the same danger that Moses encountered upon the mountain.

“And behold, I was contemplating the strange wonders of this double meaning. I said: ‘My God! My Lord! How long will You continue to show me the vision that is proper to me, under the form of these appearances? Show me the pure Uncreated, existence beyond all existence in its pure state.’ He said to me: ‘Moses and Jesus desired this spiritual dwelling, but did not attain it.’

“Then He revealed to me a single atom of light from His eternal Essence, and my spirit was almost dissolved. I feared that I was about to die. I saw our Prophet, the other prophets, all the Companions, and all the shaykhs asking God to grant me the ultimate station of Magnificence (§ 45).”
The same appeal, and the same failure, recur in another vision:

“The wonders of tawhîd appeared to me, but I was still seeing only the traces of the world of divine manifestations. I said: ‘My God! Bring me to Yourself in the state of tajrîd al-tawhîd’—that is, in the pure stripping away of everything that might qualify Your unity. Then the world of becoming appeared to me like the full moon emerging above the summit of a mountain, or like the radiance of a glowing fire burning without smoke. God caused me to enter this other world.

“I was stripped of the weaknesses imposed by ordinary ways of understanding, but I could not endure there to the end. For this dwelling was the realm of holiness, of the stripping away of all attributes (tanzîh), and of annihilation (fanâ’). Then the essential realities of the Essence (haqâ’iq al-haqîqat) became evident to me. My secret consciousness was brought to incandescence. And it was said to me: ‘This is the world of absolute Oneness (wahdâniyat), the one I proclaimed in my Book, the Quran, when I said: Nothing is like Him’ (42:9) (§ 66).”

Thus, whenever the mystic attempts to grasp transcendence itself, he is sent back to the symbol, to the divine manifestation, to the double meaning of the Veil—a veil that his innermost consciousness (sirr) will make as transparent as a mirror. Once again, flowers appear as symbols announcing the Mystery.

“Once, in the second half of the night, after seating myself upon my prayer carpet to await the appearance of the invisible Brides (‘arâ’is al-ghayb), my secret consciousness took flight into the regions of the malakût. Many times I contemplated the divine Majesty in the station of double meaning, under the awe-inspiring aspect (hayba) of His Beauty.

“But my heart was not satisfied. It longed for the unveiling of the eternal Majesty that sets ablaze the deepest secrets of consciousness and thought. And behold, I contemplated a Face more vast than all the Heavens, the Earth, the Throne, and the Korsî together. As it radiated the lights of Beauty, it transcended every idea of likeness or resemblance.

“Yet I perceived its beauty as having the appearance of a red rose—but like a world within a world, as though red roses were continually flowing forth from it, and I could see no limit to them. Then my heart remembered these words of our Prophet: ‘The red rose is a part of the divine Beauty’ (§ 71).”
Here we begin to glimpse an initiation into the secret of the double meaning inherent in created existence—an initiation that Ruzbihan will develop more fully in his doctrinal writings.

“During one of my visions… I was rising gradually through the forms of the divine manifestations. My intention was to reach the Uncreated, when I would at last be able to pass beyond the limits of these manifestations. Then I saw God in the most beautiful of forms, rising before me at the entrance to the great plain of the world of Mystery. I lost all control of myself. I wept and cried out, for this form overwhelmed me with wonder… as though white roses were being showered upon me from His Face.

“Then He became invisible, and afterwards reappeared in a form even more beautiful than the first. I went to join Him, and He spoke to me through my secret consciousness: ‘Where are we going?’ I said: ‘Towards pre-eternity.’ ‘What are you seeking?’ ‘I am seeking my annihilation (fanâ’) in the overwhelming force of what is pre-eternal, for I cannot be satisfied with the vision of appearances that bear a double meaning.’ ‘It is a long journey,’ He said. ‘I shall come with you. I shall be your travelling companion.’

“So we advanced towards what lies beyond the Throne. We made the journey through Mystery. Then He became invisible to me. An hour later He reappeared, bearing the attribute of the Jabarût, the realm of divine power, and there I was annihilated. Then He showed me a tender graciousness and said: ‘Seek me in the mystical station of love, for neither the world nor anything within the world can withstand the assaults of my Majesty.’ And I remained within the sweetness of my vision (§ 58).”

Hence the mystery of the heart: the supreme organ of the subtle spiritual body, and the centre of mystical perception. Once more, in the second half of the night, Ruzbihan meditates while contemplating the mysteries of the world of Lights.

“And behold, I saw Him upon the paths of Mystery. He held something in His hand. I said: ‘My God! What is that?’ He answered: ‘It is your heart.’ ‘So my heart has a dwelling place in Your hand?’ I asked. Then He folded my heart, so that it became like something rolled up. Afterwards He unfolded it, and now my heart stretched from the Throne to the Pleiades. I said: ‘Is this my heart?’ ‘This is your heart, and it is greater than the universe.’

“Then He carried it, just as it was, in His hand towards the regions of the malakût. I entered with Him, until I came upon the dîwân, the heavenly court of the Mystery of Mysteries. At that moment I said: ‘How far are You taking it?’ ‘To the pre-eternal world, so that I may contemplate Myself within it… and reveal Myself to it for all the eternities to come, in the form of Divinity (olûhîya).’

“I said: ‘I want to see You as You are in pre-eternity.’ ‘There is no path by which you can reach that.’ Then I pleaded with Him: ‘I want it,’ I said. And behold, the Lights of sublimity appeared. I was annihilated, utterly brought to nothing. After that, created existence could no longer offer itself to the overwhelming flood of Magnificence.

“Then my secret consciousness was addressed, and it was said to me: ‘Do you now understand the hidden meaning of these words of the Prophet: The hearts are between two of the fingers of the Merciful One, and He shapes them as He wills?’ What I saw between His fingers was the outer form of the hearts of His lovers. He shapes them—turns them—from this world towards the enclosures of His Majesty. When He withdrew into concealment… that vision left an immense joy in my deepest consciousness (sirr), until the moment when I returned to awareness (§§ 61–62).”

Little by little, the visionary is thus initiated into the secret of esoteric tawhîd. This is the secret of who truly acts in the experiences of the mystic: the eternal Companion, the divine Other Self. Until the mystic has understood this, he may suffer the pain of absence, because he does not yet know who it is that has really become absent. On the day after a spiritual concert, Ruzbihan experiences a certain relaxation. Then evening returns, and at the hour of the prayer offered during the first third of the night, he asks himself:

“Why did the wonders of Mystery not reveal themselves during yesterday’s spiritual concert (samâ‘)? Suddenly, behold, I saw God through the openings of the malakût, appearing to me with the attributes of Beauty and Majesty. I said to Him: ‘Where were You? Why did You remain invisible during the spiritual concert?’ He answered: ‘I was with you, in the very form in which you see me now.’

“Then I cried out. My secret consciousness, my intelligence, and my heart were filled with joy. ‘My God!’ I said. ‘Why, then, did I not see You?’ He answered: ‘I was behind you and above you, watching you; I was at your right and at your left, in this very form.’ Then it was as though I saw Him just as He was describing and revealing Himself. Half the night passed.

“I sought Him in the aspect of Divinity (olûhîya), without the double meaning of the Attributes and the divine Acts that reveal them. I began to plead. And behold, the lights of the Essence and the Attributes appeared to me in the pre-eternal world. There were layers of vapour rising one above another. I saw radiance upon radiance, majesty upon majesty, beauty upon beauty. I saw the holy sea (bahr al-Qods)… It seemed to me that all these Lights were smiling upon my face (§ 65).”

For there to be, at one and the same time, the unification of the One (tawhîd) and the joy of being two, we must overturn the ordinary way of seeing things, founded upon the outward understanding of religion. What the Book of the Clouding of the Divine Presence has taught us, the Diarium confirms through lived experience.

The Witness (shâhid) is no longer a separate eye looking upon God. The Witness is the eye through which God looks and reveals Himself to Himself, in the infinite variations of “the most beautiful of forms.” It is in this sense that you are His eyewitness, and that an outward understanding of tawhîd is nothing but a trick and a deception.

“And behold,” Ruzbihan relates, “I saw my soul in a state of fanâ’, of annihilation, and I was saying to myself: ‘I am the least of Your creatures. I am Your servant and the son of Your servant.’ Then the overwhelming force of divine unity and Sublimity struck against my heart. He said to me: ‘Who are you, to be a servant in relation to Me?’ I was overcome with shame before this God whom my words had no power to describe. I said: ‘What attribute could I possibly name, when I myself am merely one thing among all the things that belong to You?’

“But He said to me: ‘You are not one who truly affirms divine unity until you have forgotten both yourself and everything other than Me, from the Throne to the Pleiades.’ I remained dazzled, as though enveloped in an immense veil. I was still unable to speak when He caused me to remember something of His dhikr, the remembrance of His Name. He made me understand my annihilation in Him and my longing for Him. The great plains of Mystery grew bright, and behold, pointing to Himself, He said to me: ‘It is I who belong to you (Anâ laka).’

“Then I was seized by an emotion of ecstasy, and my heart was filled with joy. Afterwards He approached me in the form of a beautiful youth. My soul and my heart were annihilated in His grace and beauty. Coming near to me, He said: ‘Here your heart is not distressed by the declaration of divine unity. For here, tawhîd is a trick and a deception, since you are my eyewitness, and I am present in the form of grace and beauty’ (§ 77).”

The state of someone who “truly affirms divine unity” is precisely that which was attained by the last group of the Faithful in the account of the Mi‘râj, the heavenly ascent of Sari al-Saqati, which concludes the Book of the Clouding of the Divine Presence. Having remained faithful to the oneness of their Desire, this last group survived in a higher state of existence after the original company had been decimated seven times by a sevenfold ordeal.

All those who bear witness to God “objectively,” without forgetting themselves, and who believe that they themselves are the ones bearing witness, are in reality no better than polytheists. The monotheism of religion understood as a legal and social institution remains at this level. It merely places a Supreme Being (Ens supremum) above the sum of created existence. Only esoteric tawhîd, by contrast, escapes the trap of this metaphysical idolatry. The multiplicity of divine manifestations is the multiplicity of forms through which the one divine Subject appears to Himself and recognizes Himself through His creatures.

But this requires that those creatures keep their eyes open—and open upon Him alone. For then their eyes are His eyes: the eyes through which He looks, and through which He beholds Himself within them. There is therefore no longer any conflict between the One and the many. There is the multiplicity of the One, but each manifestation of that multiplicity is always, in itself, One. This is the unity of the One—or, more precisely, the mystery of unus-ambo, the two who are one.

Of both the One and the other it is equally true to say that each is the One who sees and the One who is seen. There is therefore nothing to prevent certain scenes of ecstasy that would be openly scandalous to every kind of outward religious conformity. Let us quote one more vision:

“One day I fell into the sea of Desire. The crashing waves of the Ocean of Magnificence carried me away, until I reached the mystical station in which existence beyond existence is contemplated. And behold, I saw God. Through His Beauty and Majesty, the dazzling flashes of His Face were revealed to me. I remained contemplating that beauty. I was at the height of spiritual intoxication. My spirit was almost stripped from my body, my intelligence abolished, my heart carried away, my secret consciousness annihilated…

“When dawn broke, I saw that the world seemed filled with the Divine Being. I was at once absent and present. It seemed both that I saw Him and that I was not the one who saw Him. Then, behold, He came towards me. He drew me into a dance, and I danced with Him. But as I emerged from ecstasy, I returned to consciousness at once (L. 148a).”
To close this all-too-brief examination of Ruzbihan’s Diarium spirituale, let us quote its final page. It opens with something like a threefold cry of longing and exultation:

“Then I saw Him! Then I saw Him! Then I saw Him! So many times that I could never tell their number… He caused me to travel through the highest malakût, unveiling to me the depths of pre-eternity in their state of absolute transcendence (tanzîh). He unveiled to me Beauty and Majesty. Then He revealed Himself to me under one of the forms that bear a double meaning (iltibâs).

“All the Cherubim stood before the pavilions of Magnificence. Their wonderful forms were themselves the forms of grace and beauty. Their hair was braided like that of women. The houris, dressed in robes such as the inhabitants of Paradise wear, separated and came together again. And I saw Gabriel, possessing a grace and beauty that I cannot describe. He passed very close to me, in all that grace and beauty. And I saw the Prophets and the Friends of God (Awliyâ’), immersed in the Lights flashing forth from His Majesty.

“I myself was suspended between concealment (istitar) and divine manifestation (tajallî). I was beside myself, crying out and groaning, filled with longing and driven almost mad by burning desire, like those overcome with intoxication. Then He took away all my worries and sorrows. My heart was filled with joy through His intimacy and His beauty. After that, I prayed to God for the community of Muhammad. This was at a time when a terrible epidemic had struck Shiraz. There were crowds of the dead and the sick.

“Finally, I prayed that God would deliver me: that I should no longer have to enter the palace of the Emirs. When morning came, a divine command was issued, and from that moment onward I was delivered from the sight of them and from their company (L. 51a).”
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
Chapter V The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love

The passages we have just drawn from Ruzbihan's Spiritual Diary give us a glimpse of the hidden forces at work in his innermost consciousness—the sirr, or consciousness beyond ordinary awareness—as they emerge through a succession of visionary states. He experienced these sometimes in dreams, but more often at night or around dawn, in the state between waking and sleep. Certain recurring features show us how a Sufi actually experiences and overcomes an inner conflict, not merely as a matter of theory but through the trials of spiritual life.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love

On one side stands the longing shared by all Sufis: the longing to see God personally. On the other stands the demand of tawhid as understood by outward, established religion: an abstract monotheism that treats divine oneness as though it were the unity of an object. Overcoming this demand, imposed by a collective and socially established religious norm, requires a long, arduous, and daring personal spiritual experience. That experience finds expression in the paradoxes, the “pious blasphemies,” which horrify and scandalize those devoted to the outward forms of religion.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love

Two situations embody this conflict and its resolution: the denial of the vision of God to Moses (Quran 7:139), and the prophetic testimony, “I saw my God in the most beautiful of forms.” We have already had occasion to examine one aspect of this theme in the speculative mysticism and experience of Ibn Arabi.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love

But it remains to be explored throughout the different forms of Sufism. In Ruzbihan's work, both the terms of the conflict and its resolution—a conflict that shapes the different paths taken in Islam by the religious believer and the mystic—find expression in two works of exceptional importance. One is his Commentary on the Paradoxes of the Sufis, a comprehensive account of the Sufism of his time.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love

The other is a jewel of Persian literature, which Ruzbihan called The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love. The Jasmine is no less difficult than the Commentary. It is both a work of doctrine and an autobiography. Its highly personal language, beautiful as it is, makes it hard to read and harder still to translate. Almost the entire work thinks in images. These are not rhetorical ornaments: they are concepts expressed in another form, and the book's inner dialectic works upon them just as it would upon concepts. The reader must keep a hand on both keyboards at once.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love

We can approach the book's central theme in this way. Through an inward pilgrimage along the stages of love, it resolves that conflict by leading from a legalistic, socially organized Islam to the personal, spiritual Islam of Sufism. In other words, it leads from outward tawhid—the monotheistic faith of a consciousness that takes God naively as an object—to inward tawhid, which perceives and speaks of the mystery of the Subject of divine unity. This esoteric understanding effects a genuine alchemical transformation of tawhid.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love

Official Islam no longer recognizes itself in it and refuses to acknowledge it as its own. (The existence of something called “orthodox Sufism” does nothing to diminish the meaning of the rejection made here in the name of religious legalism.) Because this transformation overturns our whole perspective, the Book of the Clouding has already announced it in certain striking formulations: the mystic must himself become the eye through which God beholds Himself. This requires a return to a state preceding the division between subject and object, a state in which the Divine Being can neither be turned into an object nor made into a social institution. In that state, the Divine is experienced as the absolute Subject for and through each individual existence.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love

That state—the very meaning of inward tawhid—is what the Sufis found expressed in a Neoplatonic formula, known to them through the work called the Theology of Aristotle: the Divine Being is at once love, the lover, and the beloved.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love

Consider the distance between the one God affirmed by the literal faith of official Islam and the Sufi understanding of divine unity as absolute subjectivity: absolute because it stands in no relation to anything other than itself. The distance between the two reveals the scale of the spiritual transformation that Sufism brings about in relation to the outward religion of the Law.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love

Now, if the divine mystery offered to inward religion is expressed as the unity of love, lover, and beloved, then there can be only one path by which the initiate approaches and experiences that mystery. The formula itself tells us what the path is.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love

Inward tawhid can be understood, experienced, and realized only in and through love. Human love—eros—opens the way to it, because human love is the one actual experience which, at its furthest limit, can give an intimation of, and sometimes bring about, the unity of love, lover, and beloved. This is the command Ruzbihan heard in one of his visions: “Seek Me in the mystical station of love.”
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love

Here, too, lies the profound difference between the spirituality of Ruzbihan and those like him, and that of the Christian ascetic in general. The difference also sets them apart from the Sufis whom Ruzbihan calls the “pious ascetics” (sohhad), as opposed to the faithful in love. These are, broadly speaking, devotees for whom human beauty—and beauty perceived through the senses generally—is a snare, perhaps even a temptation from the devil, and for whom human love is not a way toward divine love but an obstacle to it.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love

The distinctive character of Iranian Sufism lies here. It entails a challenge, and an individual ethic that is heroic and secret, embodied in the javanmard, the knight of the soul. For Ruzbihan, as for Ahmad Ghazali, Fakhr Eraqi, and Hafez, there is only one love.
